PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__PHQ-9 (Depressio:
The PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9) is a 9-item self-report questionnaire that maps directly onto the DSM diagnostic criteria for a major depressive episode. It is used in primary care and general settings to screen for depression, grade its severity, and monitor response to treatment over time. Each item asks how often a symptom has bothered the patient over the last 2 weeks, giving a total score from 0 to 27 that guides stepped care.

1INDICATION — when and why it is used

The PHQ-9 is used to case-find and quantify depression in patients where low mood is suspected, and to objectively track change once treatment (talking therapy or antidepressant) has begun. Because its 9 items mirror the DSM-5 symptom criteria, it doubles as both a screening tool and a severity/monitoring measure, unlike simpler two-item screens.

Validated, free, and quick (2–5 minutes) — suited to busy primary care.
Maps to DSM criteria, so it supports (not replaces) clinical diagnosis.
Repeatable, so it charts response and remission across appointments.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — administration & scoring

The patient rates each of the 9 items for the last 2 weeks on a 0–3 frequency scale: not at all (0), several days (1), more than half the days (2), nearly every day (3). The nine item scores are summed to give a total of 0–27.

🧪Core mood items
Little interest/pleasure (anhedonia) and feeling down/hopeless.
🧪Somatic items
Sleep, energy, appetite, and psychomotor change.
🧪Cognitive items
Poor concentration and feelings of worthlessness/guilt.
🚩Item 9
Thoughts of self-harm or being better off dead — the safety item.

A commonly examined functional add-on question asks how difficult these problems have made daily functioning, though it does not count toward the numerical total.

3INTERPRETATION — severity bands

The total score is read against established severity bands, which guide stepped-care decisions:

0–4→None / minimal depression
5–9→Mild depression
10–14→Moderate depression
15–19→Moderately severe depression
20–27→Severe depression
≥10→Threshold at which clinically significant depression is likely — consider active treatment

A fall of around 5 points, or dropping into a lower band, is used as a marker of meaningful treatment response.

4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
It is a screening/severity aid, not a stand-alone diagnosis — clinical assessment is still required.
Somatic items (sleep, appetite, energy, concentration) can be inflated by physical illness, chronic pain, or old age, overestimating severity.
Self-report is vulnerable to under-reporting, poor literacy, language barriers, and cognitive impairment.
The total score can be low even when suicide risk is high — the number never overrides clinical judgement.
🚩 Item 9 screens for suicidal ideation. Any positive response (thoughts that the patient would be better off dead, or of self-harm) mandates an immediate risk assessment regardless of the total score. Never rely on the number alone — a low total does not exclude significant suicide risk.
🎓 PHQ-9 scores range 0–27; the cut-offs 5 / 10 / 15 / 20 mark mild / moderate / moderately-severe / severe depression. Item 9 flags suicidal ideation and always triggers a risk assessment, whatever the total.
Score band → stepped care (NICE NG222)→less severe (PHQ-9 <16) → guided self-help, CBT or behavioural activation (do not routinely start an antidepressant); more severe (≥16) → offer an antidepressant (SSRI first-line, e.g. sertraline) and/or high-intensity psychological therapy (CBT/IPT) by patient choice. Depressive disorders ›
Starting an SSRI→review at 2 weeks — or 1 week if under 25 or any suicide risk (early activation/ideation); continue ≥6 months after remission. Track recovery by repeating the PHQ-9 (remission = <5). Psychotropic drugs ›
Item 9 positive (self-harm thoughts)→regardless of the total → immediate risk assessment: collaborative safety plan, means restriction, involve family/carer; urgent same-day crisis-team/CMHT referral or A&E if high/acute risk, otherwise primary care with short-interval follow-up. Self-harm & suicide risk ›
Refer to secondary care (CMHT)→severe or psychotic depression, significant self-neglect/risk, treatment resistance, or diagnostic uncertainty (e.g. bipolar).
🎓 Exam pearl. Score drives the offer: <16 → psychological/self-help; ≥16 → SSRI ± high-intensity therapy. A positive item 9 mandates an immediate risk assessment whatever the total. Under-25s on a new SSRI are reviewed at 1 week.
PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__GAD-7 (Anxiety):
The GAD-7 (Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7) is a 7-item self-report questionnaire used to screen for and measure the severity of generalised anxiety over the preceding 2 weeks. It is not diagnostic on its own but is a validated, quick tool widely used in UK primary care and IAPT (NHS Talking Therapies) services. Although designed for GAD, it is also sensitive to panic disorder, social anxiety disorder and PTSD, and is commonly paired with the PHQ-9 because anxiety and depression frequently coexist.

1INDICATION — when and why it is used

The GAD-7 is used to case-find and quantify anxiety in patients presenting with worry, restlessness, irritability, poor sleep or somatic tension, and to track response to treatment over time. It gives an objective, repeatable severity score that supports stepped-care decisions and monitors change during psychological therapy or medication titration.

Self-completed in under 3 minutes, requiring no clinician administration.
Validated in primary care; sensitive to GAD, panic, social anxiety and PTSD.
Frequently administered alongside the PHQ-9 for co-existing depression.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — scoring the 7 items

The patient rates how often they have been bothered by each of 7 core anxiety symptoms (e.g. feeling nervous or on edge, not being able to stop or control worrying, trouble relaxing, becoming easily annoyed) over the last 2 weeks. Each item is scored on a 4-point frequency scale.

Not at all→0 points
Several days→1 point
More than half the days→2 points
Nearly every day→3 points

The 7 item scores are summed to give a total of 0–21. A separate final question on functional impairment (how difficult symptoms make daily life) is recorded but does not count toward the total.

3INTERPRETATION — severity bands and thresholds

The total maps onto four severity bands, with a score of ≥10 the usual threshold for likely GAD warranting further assessment.

0–4→Minimal anxiety
5–9→Mild anxiety
10–14→Moderate anxiety
15–21→Severe anxiety
Score ≥10→Likely GAD — confirm with clinical assessment
🧪GAD-7
Anxiety severity, total 0–21
🧪PHQ-9
Paired screen for co-existing depression
4PITFALLS AND LIMITATIONS

The GAD-7 relies on honest self-report and reflects only the last 2 weeks, so it can be inflated by transient stressors or under-reported by patients minimising symptoms. A raised score is never sufficient to diagnose GAD: the clinician must confirm persistent, excessive, hard-to-control worry lasting most days for at least 6 months, and must actively exclude organic and substance-related mimics of anxiety.

🚩 The GAD-7 is a screening and severity tool, NOT a diagnosis. A raised score requires clinical assessment to confirm GAD and to exclude organic mimics — hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, phaeochromocytoma, substance or caffeine use, and medication effects (e.g. salbutamol, steroids) — before anxiety is treated as primary.
🎓 GAD-7 scores 0–21; the cut-offs 5 / 10 / 15 mark mild / moderate / severe. A score ≥10 suggests likely GAD and further assessment. Screen for co-existing depression with the PHQ-9 and always exclude organic causes of anxiety.
Score band → NICE stepped care→Step 1 education/active monitoring → Step 2 low-intensity (guided self-help, psychoeducation) → Step 3 high-intensity CBT or a drug — SSRI first-line (e.g. sertraline) → Step 4 SNRI (duloxetine/venlafaxine) or pregabalin, then specialist referral. Anxiety disorders ›
Avoid long-term benzodiazepines→only short-term in a crisis (dependence risk) — not for chronic GAD. Review a new SSRI at ~2–4 weeks, watching for early anxiety worsening/suicidality in the young. Psychotropic drugs ›
GAD-2 (ultra-brief screen)→the first 2 items (score 0–6); a score ≥3 prompts the full GAD-7.
🎓 Exam pearl. First-line drug for GAD is an SSRI (sertraline); escalate to SNRI or pregabalin, not regular benzodiazepines. Screen with GAD-2 (≥3 → full GAD-7), and always exclude organic mimics (thyroid, arrhythmia, phaeo, caffeine/substances).
PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__Y-BOCS (OCD):
The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) is a clinician-administered, semi-structured rating scale that measures the severity of obsessive-compulsive disorder independently of the content of a patient's obsessions and compulsions. It is the gold-standard instrument for grading OCD severity at baseline and for tracking response to treatment (CBT or medication) over time. It is a severity measure, not a diagnostic test.

1INDICATION — when and why it is used

Used in patients with an established or suspected diagnosis of OCD to quantify how disabling their symptoms are and to monitor change. Because it scores the burden of symptoms rather than their theme (contamination, checking, symmetry, intrusive thoughts), the same scale applies whatever the content. It is the standard primary outcome measure in OCD treatment trials.

Grades baseline severity to guide treatment intensity.
Tracks response — a ≥25–35% fall in total score is the usual definition of treatment response.
Content-independent, so it works across all OCD symptom subtypes.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — structure and scoring

A symptom checklist is completed first to identify the patient's specific obsessions and compulsions. The severity scale then has 10 items: 5 rating obsessions and 5 rating compulsions. Each item is scored 0–4, giving a total of 0–40.

The five dimensions rated for both obsessions and compulsions are:

🕒Time
Hours per day occupied by symptoms
🚧Interference
Disruption to work, social and family life
😰Distress
Anxiety caused by symptoms
✊Resistance
Effort made to resist symptoms
🎚️Control
Degree of control over symptoms
3INTERPRETATION — severity bands

The total score maps to five severity bands:

0–7→Subclinical
8–15→Mild OCD
16–23→Moderate OCD
24–31→Severe OCD
32–40→Extreme OCD

Under NICE, mild functional impairment is offered low-intensity CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP); more marked impairment warrants an SSRI and/or more intensive ERP-based CBT. SSRIs for OCD are often needed at higher doses and for longer (up to 12 weeks) than in depression before a response is judged.

4PITFALLS AND LIMITATIONS
It measures severity only — it does not make the diagnosis and does not assess risk.
Insight is variable; where insight is lost, distinguish OCD from a psychotic disorder.
Do not confuse OCD with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD), which is ego-syntonic and lacks true obsessions and compulsions.
Score can be inflated or deflated by co-morbid depression affecting how distress and interference are reported.
🚩 The Y-BOCS grades severity but is not diagnostic and does not assess risk. Always screen separately for co-morbid depression and suicidality. Distinguish OCD from OCPD (ego-syntonic personality traits) and from psychosis where insight into the senselessness of symptoms is lost.
🎓 Y-BOCS = 10 items (5 obsessions + 5 compulsions), each 0–4, total 0–40, rating time, interference, distress, resistance and control. Treat OCD with ERP-based CBT and/or a high-dose SSRI. It grades severity, but it is not diagnostic.
Severity band → NICE stepped care→mild (8–15) → low-intensity CBT with ERP; moderate (16–23) → an SSRI or intensive CBT/ERP; severe/extreme (≥24) → combined SSRI + CBT/ERP and referral to specialist OCD services. OCD / anxiety disorders ›
OCD drug treatment→SSRI first-line (higher dose and a longer trial — judge response at ~12 weeks, not the 4–6 of depression); if ineffective/not tolerated → clomipramine (a TCA, second-line). Psychotropic drugs ›
What is ERP?→exposure and response prevention: graded exposure to the feared trigger while preventing the compulsion, so anxiety habituates without the ritual.
Monitoring→repeat the Y-BOCS to track response — a ~25–35% fall in total score = a meaningful response.
🎓 Exam pearl. Band drives the plan: mild → ERP; moderate → SSRI or ERP; severe → SSRI + ERP + specialist referral. SSRI first-line (12-week trial), clomipramine second-line. ERP = exposure + preventing the ritual.
PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__EPDS / Whooley (:
The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) and the Whooley questions are complementary case-finding tools for perinatal (antenatal and postnatal) depression. The EPDS is a validated 10-item self-report questionnaire; the two Whooley questions are an ultra-brief screen NICE recommends at the booking appointment and postnatally. Together they identify women who need fuller assessment for depression during pregnancy and the first postnatal year.

1INDICATION — when and why they are used

Perinatal depression affects roughly 1 in 10 women and is under-detected because low mood is wrongly normalised in new mothers. NICE recommends asking the Whooley questions at first contact in pregnancy (booking) and postnatally as a rapid, low-burden case-finding step, with the EPDS (or PHQ-9) used to assess further when screening is positive.

Whooley = fast triage that almost anyone can administer in under a minute.
EPDS = a structured 10-item scale that quantifies symptom severity and tracks response.
The EPDS deliberately avoids somatic items (sleep, appetite, fatigue) that overlap with normal new-parenthood, improving specificity.
2HOW THEY ARE PERFORMED — administration and scoring

The two Whooley questions cover the past month: (1) “Have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?” and (2) “Have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?” (low mood + anhedonia). A “yes” to either is positive; NICE suggests a third “help” question — “Is this something you feel you need or want help with?”

The EPDS is self-completed: 10 items, each scored 0–3, giving a total of 0–30. It asks about the past 7 days. Item 10 specifically asks about thoughts of self-harm.

🧪Whooley Q1
Low/depressed mood over the past month
🧪Whooley Q2
Anhedonia — little interest or pleasure
📋EPDS
10 items, each 0–3, total 0–30, past 7 days
⚠️EPDS item 10
Thoughts of self-harm — any positive answer
3INTERPRETATION — thresholds and what they mean
Either Whooley question positive→Ask the third “help” question and assess further with EPDS or PHQ-9
EPDS ≥10–13→Possible depression — clinical assessment needed (local cut-offs vary)
EPDS ≥13→Suggests probable major (more severe) depressive illness
EPDS item 10 positive (any score >0)→Urgent risk assessment regardless of total score

Screening tools do not diagnose — a positive result triggers a full clinical assessment. Crucially, distinguish three entities:

Baby blues — peaks around days 3–10, tearful/labile but self-limiting; needs reassurance, not treatment.
Postnatal depression — persistent low mood/anhedonia, typically emerging within weeks to months; managed like depression (talking therapy, and antidepressants if moderate-severe).
Postpartum psychosis — abrupt severe illness within days to 2 weeks; a psychiatric emergency.
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS AND SAFETY
A screen is not a diagnosis — sensitivity/specificity depend on the cut-off, and a negative EPDS does not exclude illness if clinical concern is high.
The EPDS may perform poorly where language or literacy limit self-completion, or when women under-report for fear of stigma or child-protection consequences.
Never treat a total score in isolation: item 10 (self-harm) overrides the total and mandates immediate risk assessment.
Screening must always be linked to a clear referral pathway to perinatal mental-health services.
🚩 Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency. Suspect it with abrupt onset within days to 2 weeks of delivery: confusion, mania, rapidly fluctuating mood, delusions, hallucinations, or thoughts of harming herself or the baby. This needs same-day specialist perinatal assessment and usually admission — ideally to a mother-and-baby unit. Any positive EPDS item 10 or any thought of harm to self or infant is a red flag requiring urgent action.
🎓 Remember the pairing: Whooley = 2-question screen (down + anhedonia over the past month, plus a third help question); EPDS = 10-item scale, score 0–30, cut-off around 10–13. Item 10 flags self-harm and overrides the total. Always separate baby blues (self-limiting, days 3–10) from postnatal depression and from the emergency of postpartum psychosis.
Treating postnatal depression→mild → guided self-help / CBT in primary care; moderate–severe (or item-10 positive) → specialist perinatal mental-health referral + an SSRI — sertraline is preferred if breastfeeding (low breast-milk levels). Depressive disorders ›
Highest risk for puerperal psychosis→pre-existing bipolar disorder, a previous puerperal psychosis, or family history (recurrence ~1 in 2) → flag for antenatal perinatal planning. Bipolar disorder › Postpartum complications ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Treat PND like depression but choose the drug for breastfeeding — sertraline is preferred. A woman with bipolar disorder or previous puerperal psychosis is high-risk and needs antenatal perinatal-team planning.
PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__SCOFF (Eating Di:
The SCOFF questionnaire is a brief 5-item, yes/no screening tool designed to raise suspicion of an eating disorder — principally anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa — in primary care and general medical settings. It is quick, memorable and validated for use by non-specialists, but it is a screen, not a diagnosis: a positive result should prompt fuller clinical assessment of weight, physical health and risk.

1INDICATION — when and why it is used

Eating disorders are common, frequently concealed, and carry the highest mortality of any psychiatric illness. Patients rarely present with the disorder itself, instead reporting fatigue, amenorrhoea, gastrointestinal upset or low mood. SCOFF gives a clinician a rapid, structured prompt to screen opportunistically when there is clinical suspicion (low or fluctuating weight, young patient, dental erosion, electrolyte abnormality). Its value lies in sensitivity — catching cases that would otherwise be missed — rather than confirming a diagnosis.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — the five questions

The five items are self-administered or asked directly. The acronym SCOFF maps to each question:

🤢Sick
Do you make yourself Sick because you feel uncomfortably full?
🎛️Control
Do you worry you have lost Control over how much you eat?
⚖️One stone
Have you recently lost more than One stone (~6.35 kg) in a 3-month period?
🪞Fat
Do you believe yourself to be Fat when others say you are too thin?
🍽️Food
Would you say that Food dominates your life?
Each "yes" scores 1 point; each "no" scores 0. Maximum score is 5.
Takes under two minutes and requires no equipment.
3INTERPRETATION — the score bands
Score 0–1→Screen negative — eating disorder unlikely, but reassess if clinical suspicion persists
Score ≥2 of 5 "yes"→Screen positive — likely anorexia or bulimia nervosa; warrants further assessment
Any positive screen→Assess BMI, physical complications and risk — SCOFF is a screen, not a diagnosis
At the ≥2 cut-off, sensitivity is high (~85–100%) for anorexia and bulimia, making it a good rule-out tool.
A positive screen mandates a full history, physical examination, weight/BMI, and bloods including electrolytes.
4PITFALLS, COMPLICATIONS & SAFETY

SCOFF does not measure severity or medical risk — a patient can score low yet be dangerously unwell. The key complications to screen for actively are electrolyte disturbance and cardiovascular instability. Recurrent vomiting or laxative misuse causes hypokalaemia (risk of arrhythmia) and a metabolic alkalosis; severe malnutrition depletes phosphate, potassium and magnesium, setting the scene for refeeding syndrome once nutrition is restored.

Self-induced vomiting / laxatives→Hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis — check U&Es and ECG
Very low BMI, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia→Medical instability — consider urgent admission using a risk framework (MEED/MARSIPAN)
🚩 Screen every positive case for medical instability and the risk of refeeding syndrome when re-nourishing a severely malnourished patient. Watch for falling phosphate, potassium and magnesium. Bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, a very low BMI and electrolyte derangement signal a medical emergency requiring admission — stratify with a formal framework such as MEED (Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders) / MARSIPAN.
🎓 SCOFF: ≥2 of 5 "yes" answers screens positive for an eating disorder. It is not diagnostic — assess BMI, electrolytes and risk, and beware refeeding syndrome (low phosphate / potassium / magnesium) when re-nourishing.
PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__AUDIT / CAGE (Al:
CAGE and AUDIT are validated screening questionnaires for detecting problem drinking. CAGE is a rapid 4-item screen suggesting alcohol dependence, while the AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test) is the WHO's 10-item tool quantifying consumption, dependence symptoms and alcohol-related harm; its 3-item consumption-only version (AUDIT-C) is widely used in busy clinical settings. They stratify a patient's drinking so clinicians can decide between brief advice, structured intervention or specialist referral.

1INDICATION — why screen

Alcohol misuse is common, frequently unrecognised, and drives a huge burden of physical, psychiatric and social harm. Structured screening detects hazardous and harmful drinking before overt dependence or organ damage, and is recommended opportunistically (new registrations, A&E attendances, mental health assessments) and in patients with relevant presentations such as hypertension, seizures, deranged liver enzymes or low mood.

CAGE — brief, memorable, good for detecting probable dependence.
AUDIT — most sensitive, grades the whole spectrum from hazardous use to dependence.
AUDIT-C — first 3 consumption items, quick to embed in routine practice.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Each is a self-report or clinician-administered questionnaire; no bloods or examination are needed.

✂️C — Cut down
Ever felt you should cut down?
😠A — Annoyed
Annoyed by others criticising your drinking?
😔G — Guilty
Ever felt guilty about your drinking?
👁️E — Eye-opener
Ever had a morning drink to steady nerves / cure a hangover?

CAGE scores 1 point per “yes” (0–4). AUDIT has 10 items each scored 0–4 giving a total of 0–40; items 1–3 cover consumption, 4–6 dependence, 7–10 alcohol-related harm. AUDIT-C uses only the first three consumption questions, scored 0–12.

3INTERPRETATION — the cut-offs
CAGE ≥ 2 positive answers→Suggests problem drinking / probable alcohol dependence — assess further
AUDIT 0–7→Low-risk drinking — no intervention needed
AUDIT ≥ 8→Hazardous / harmful drinking — give brief intervention
AUDIT ≥ 20→Possible dependence — refer for specialist assessment
AUDIT-C ≥ 5 (men) / ≥ 4 (women)→Screens positive — proceed to full AUDIT
4ACTION, PITFALLS & SAFETY
Hazardous / harmful use → structured brief advice (feedback, goal-setting, motivational support).
Dependence → assisted (medically supervised) withdrawal plus relapse-prevention pharmacotherapy such as acamprosate, plus psychosocial support.
Give oral or parenteral thiamine to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy in anyone drinking harmfully or undergoing withdrawal.

Limitations: both rely on honest self-report and can be falsely reassuring in patients minimising intake; CAGE detects lifetime dependence but is insensitive to hazardous use and binge patterns; screening is not diagnostic and must be paired with a full history and examination.

🚩 Never advise a dependent drinker to stop abruptly without cover. Sudden cessation can precipitate alcohol WITHDRAWAL — seizures early on and delirium tremens at 48–72 h (confusion, autonomic instability, hallucinations), which is life-threatening. Treat withdrawal with a benzodiazepine (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) and give PARENTERAL THIAMINE (Pabrinex) — and never give glucose before thiamine, as a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
🎓 CAGE ≥ 2 or AUDIT ≥ 8 screens positive; AUDIT grades hazardous, harmful and dependent use. Treat withdrawal with benzodiazepines and always give thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__Cognitive Screen:
Cognitive screens are brief, standardised bedside tests that quantify cognition to screen for dementia and delirium and to track change over time. They are quick to administer and give a numerical score against a cut-off, but they are screening tools, not diagnostic tests — a low score flags the need for fuller assessment rather than confirming a diagnosis. The commonest UK instruments are the AMTS, MMSE, MoCA and 6-CIT.

1INDICATION — when and why they are used

Used whenever cognitive impairment is suspected: memory complaints, functional decline, an acute confusional state, or routine screening of older inpatients. They convert a subjective “seems muddled” into an objective, repeatable number, allowing comparison against a threshold and monitoring of change (e.g. progression of dementia or resolution of delirium).

Screen for dementia and delirium, and monitor cognitive trajectory.
Choose the tool by setting: ward/acute vs memory clinic vs primary care.
A score is only meaningful alongside history, function and collateral.
2HOW THEY ARE PERFORMED — the main tools

Each is a structured set of questions/tasks scored to a total. Optimise conditions first: hearing aids and glasses on, quiet setting, patient's usual language, and note educational background.

🧪AMTS
10 items, /10. Fast ward-based screen (age, time, address recall, orientation, memory).
🧪MMSE
/30, ~10 min. Orientation, registration, attention, recall, language, praxis.
🧪MoCA
/30. Adds trail-making, cube/clock, abstraction — sensitive for executive/visuospatial.
🧪6-CIT
Short primary-care screen; scored inversely so a HIGHER score = worse.
3INTERPRETATION — cut-offs and what they mean

Compare the total to the tool's threshold. Lower is worse for AMTS/MMSE/MoCA; the 6-CIT runs the opposite way.

AMTS ≤6/10→Suggests cognitive impairment; quick ward flag prompting fuller assessment
MMSE <24/30→Suggests impairment; weak for frontal/executive deficits and mild cases
MoCA <26/30→Abnormal; most sensitive for MILD cognitive impairment and executive/visuospatial domains
6-CIT (higher score)→Worse cognition; a raised score in primary care prompts referral
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY

A low score is a starting point, not an answer. It should prompt formal cognitive assessment, collateral history, reversible-cause bloods and neuroimaging to identify the dementia subtype and exclude treatable mimics.

Screens do not distinguish delirium from dementia — assess attention (e.g. 4AT) and exclude acute delirium first.
Reversible causes to exclude: B12/folate deficiency, thyroid dysfunction, hypercalcaemia, infection, depression (pseudodementia), and culprit medications.
Education, language and sensory (hearing/vision) impairment all confound scores — interpret in context.
🚩 A cognitive screen alone cannot separate DELIRIUM from dementia. Always exclude and treat acute delirium (assess attention / use the 4AT) before diagnosing dementia, and screen for reversible causes — B12/folate, thyroid, calcium, infection, depression and medication. Educational level, language and sensory impairment confound every score.
🎓 Remember the thresholds: AMTS ≤6/10, MMSE <24/30, MoCA <26/30 suggest impairment. MoCA is the most sensitive for mild cognitive impairment. All are screens — not diagnostic — and delirium plus reversible causes must be excluded first.
PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__Capacity Assessm:
The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA) is the statutory framework in England & Wales for deciding whether an adult (16 and over) can make a specific decision at a specific time. Capacity is assessed using a 2-stage test underpinned by 5 statutory principles. It is not a diagnosis of a person but a judgement about one decision — a patient may have capacity to choose a meal yet lack it for a major operation.

1INDICATION — when capacity is assessed

Assess capacity whenever a person's ability to make a particular decision is in doubt — consent to or refusal of treatment, discharge planning, finances, or placement. The starting point is always the presumption of capacity; you only formally assess when there is a reasonable basis to question it.

Applies to those 16 and over; under-16s are governed by Gillick competence.
Triggered by a specific decision, not by a label such as “dementia” or “psychosis”.
2THE 5 STATUTORY PRINCIPLES
✅Presume capacity
Assume capacity unless established otherwise
🤝Support to decide
All practicable help given before deeming someone unable
🎲Unwise decisions
An unwise choice does not itself prove incapacity
❤️Best interests
Acts for someone lacking capacity must be in their best interests
🕊️Least restrictive
Choose the option least restrictive of rights and freedom
3THE 2-STAGE TEST — interpretation
Stage 1 (diagnostic)→Is there an impairment of, or disturbance in, the functioning of the mind or brain? (e.g. dementia, delirium, intoxication, brain injury, severe mental illness)
Stage 2 (functional)→Because of it, is the person UNABLE to do any ONE of the four abilities below?
UNDERSTAND→Cannot understand the relevant information (nature, purpose, risks, benefits, alternatives)
RETAIN→Cannot retain it long enough to make the decision
USE / WEIGH→Cannot use or weigh the information as part of deciding
COMMUNICATE→Cannot communicate the decision by any means (talking, signing, blinking)
Both stages positive→Lacks capacity for THIS decision → act in best interests, least restrictively, checking for LPA / advance decision / IMCA
4PITFALLS, SAFEGUARDS & ACTING ON THE OUTCOME
Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific — it can fluctuate (e.g. delirium), so reassess.
If lacking capacity, check for a Lasting Power of Attorney (health & welfare), a valid Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT), or the need for an IMCA where there is no one to consult on serious decisions.
A best-interests decision must consider the person's past and present wishes, feelings, beliefs and values.
Depriving someone of liberty in their best interests requires separate authorisation (DoLS / Liberty Protection Safeguards).
🚩 Capacity is decision- and time-specific — do NOT label a person as globally “incapable”. A person may make an unwise decision and still have full capacity. A valid and applicable ADRT refusing treatment must be respected even if the refusal risks death. For under-16s (and often 16–17s) different rules such as Gillick competence apply.
🎓 MCA 2-stage test: (1) impairment of mind/brain, then (2) unable to Understand, Retain, Use/weigh, or Communicate. Capacity is decision- and time-specific; unwise decisions do NOT equal lack of capacity; if capacity is absent, act in best interests and least restrictively.
PSYCHIATRY & COGNITION__Mental Health Ac:
The Mental Health Act 1983 (England & Wales, amended 2007) provides the legal framework to detain and treat a person with a mental disorder in hospital against their will, where this is necessary for their own health or safety or for the protection of others. It is used only when informal (voluntary) admission is not appropriate and no less restrictive option exists. Detention is delivered through numbered “sections”, each with its own purpose, duration and required assessors.

1INDICATION — when the Act is used

Two conditions must both be met: the person has (or is suspected to have) a mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting assessment/treatment in hospital, AND detention is needed for their health, safety or the protection of others. The guiding principle is least restriction — always prefer informal admission or community care if safe.

An AMHP (Approved Mental Health Professional, usually a social worker) coordinates most civil detentions and makes the application.
Assessment usually requires two doctors, one of whom is Section 12 approved (specially trained in the Act, often a psychiatrist).
The Act covers detention and treatment of mental disorder — it does not authorise treatment of unrelated physical illness against a capacitous person's wishes.
2THE CIVIL SECTIONS — assessment vs treatment vs emergency

The three core hospital-admission sections differ by purpose, duration and how many doctors are needed.

Section 2→Admission for ASSESSMENT — up to 28 days, NOT renewable; needs 2 doctors + AMHP; used when diagnosis/treatment plan unclear
Section 3→Admission for TREATMENT — up to 6 months, renewable; needs 2 doctors + AMHP; used when the disorder is already known
Section 4→EMERGENCY admission — 72 hours, only 1 doctor + AMHP; used when waiting for a second doctor would cause undesirable delay
3HOLDING & POLICE POWERS

Holding powers buy time to arrange a full assessment for someone already in hospital; police powers deal with people in the community.

Section 5(2)→DOCTOR'S holding power — 72 hours; detains a voluntary INPATIENT while a Section 2/3 assessment is organised
Section 5(4)→NURSE'S holding power — 6 hours; used when no doctor is immediately available; converts to 5(2) on doctor review
Section 136→POLICE power — remove a person from a PUBLIC place to a place of safety, up to 24 hours, for MHA assessment
Section 135→Magistrate's WARRANT — allows police to enter a PRIVATE property to remove a person to a place of safety

4PITFALLS, TREATMENT SAFEGUARDS & RIGHTS
Holding powers do not authorise treatment — they only prevent the patient leaving until a proper assessment occurs.
Section 5(2)/5(4) cannot be used in A&E or the community — the person must be an admitted hospital inpatient (A&E patients are not yet “admitted”).
Prolonged medication (beyond 3 months) and ECT require additional safeguards, e.g. a SOAD (Second Opinion Appointed Doctor); ECT cannot be given to a capacitous patient who refuses it except in emergencies.
Detained patients have rights of appeal to a Mental Health Tribunal and to an IMHA (Independent Mental Health Advocate).
🚩 Holding powers 5(2) and 5(4) apply ONLY to patients ALREADY ADMITTED to a hospital ward — NOT to A&E or the community — and do NOT authorise treatment. Section 136 applies only to a PUBLIC place (use Section 135 for a private home). Treatment against a patient's will has its own safeguards (SOAD/second opinion for prolonged medication, separate rules for ECT). Always choose the LEAST restrictive option and involve an AMHP.
